question: What does peripheral neuropathy primarily affect in the human body?

options.A: The gray matter of the spinal cord
options.B: Only autonomic centers in the brainstem
options.C: The cerebral cortex and basal ganglia
options.D: Nerves outside the brain and spinal cord

explanation: Peripheral neuropathies specifically target the peripheral nervous system, which connects the central nervous system to limbs and organs. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h1)

question: A diabetic patient in the ward reports a loss of sensation in both feet. What process does this indicate?

options.A: Enhanced autonomic control of the lower extremities
options.B: Disruption of sensory communication to the central nervous system
options.C: complete regeneration of damaged muscle fibers
options.D: Acute inflammation of the cerebral motor cortex

explanation: Nerve damage interrupts the pathway that transmits sensory signals from the periphery up to the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h1)

question: Name the outermost connective tissue layer that encloses an entire peripheral nerve trunk.
explanation: The epineurium forms the tough outer protective covering of the whole nerve trunk. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h2)

question: Why is the presence of a myelin sheath important for a nerve fiber?

options.A: It prevents muscle atrophy during prolonged periods of immobility
options.B: It produces neurotransmitters for the neuromuscular junction
options.C: It provides the primary blood supply directly to the nerve cells
options.D: It speeds up the transmission of electrical impulses along the axon

explanation: Myelin acts as an electrical insulator, allowing impulses to jump along the axon and travel much faster. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h2)

question: What type of neuropathy involves damage to a single nerve, often caused by trauma or entrapment?
explanation: Mononeuropathy affects only one specific nerve, such as in carpal tunnel syndrome. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h3)

question: A malnourished patient presents with symmetrical burning pain in both lower limbs. Which category of neuropathy fits this presentation?
explanation: Deficiencies in essential vitamins frequently trigger symmetrical, painful sensory symptoms in distal extremities. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h3)

question: What is the term for a complete transection of both the nerve axon and its supporting connective tissue?
explanation: Neurotmesis represents the most severe classification of nerve injury where continuity of the nerve is entirely lost. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h4)

question: Why does neurapraxia resolve quickly without permanent structural damage?

options.A: The axon remains intact without structural degeneration
options.B: The myelin sheath dissolves and instantly regenerates overnight
options.C: Schwann cells rapidly multiply to form a new nerve trunk
options.D: Local blood vessels bypass the injury site completely

explanation: Because the axon is not severed or structurally broken, normal conduction usually returns once pressure or ischemia is relieved. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h4)

question: Which symptom pattern is most characteristic of distal symmetrical polyneuropathy?
explanation: Distal polyneuropathies typically affect the feet and hands first, creating a stocking-glove pattern of numbness and tingling. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h5)

question: What finding during a physical examination indicates lower motor neuron involvement from a nerve disorder?

options.A: Diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes
options.B: Spastic paralysis of the affected limb

explanation: Damage to peripheral motor nerves interrupts the reflex arc, leading to hyporeflexia or flaccid muscle tone. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h5)

question: What do nerve conduction studies primarily measure?

options.A: Chemical composition of the cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Blood flow velocity through major peripheral arteries
options.C: Speed and strength of electrical signals in a nerve
options.D: Bone density within the surrounding limb structures

explanation: Nerve conduction studies assess how fast and effectively electrical impulses travel across tested nerve segments. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h6)

question: Why would a physician order a fasting blood glucose test for a patient presenting with peripheral neuropathy?

options.A: Glucose levels measure the exact rate of myelin sheath repair
options.B: Elevated blood sugar rules out all forms of traumatic injury
options.C: High blood sugar directly increases nerve conduction velocity
options.D: Diabetes mellitus is a leading systemic cause of nerve damage

explanation: Screening for diabetes is essential because chronic hyperglycemia is one of the most common causes of peripheral neuropathy worldwide. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h6)

question: Which medication class is commonly prescribed as a first-line treatment for neuropathic pain?
explanation: Drugs like gabapentin and pregabalin help stabilize overactive nerve membranes, reducing chronic burning pain. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h7)

question: A patient asks why they are given an antidepressant when they do not feel depressed, but have burning foot pain. What is the best clinical reasoning?

options.A: Certain antidepressants alter neurotransmitter levels in the spinal cord to reduce pain signals
options.B: The drug acts as a mild sedative to prevent nighttime muscle cramps
options.C: The medication is primarily intended to lower the patient's blood pressure
options.D: Antidepressants accelerate the complete physical regeneration of severed muscle fibers

explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants enhance descending inhibitory pain pathways in the central nervous system, helping to dull neuropathic pain. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h7)

question: A patient with severe peripheral neuropathy asks why they must check their feet every day using a mirror. What is the primary reason for this instruction?

options.A: Loss of sensation prevents them from feeling injuries or pressure sores
options.B: Daily inspection increases blood circulation to the lower extremities
options.C: Visual checks stimulate dormant sensory nerves in the soles
options.D: It helps monitor the growth of toenails during long-term bed rest

explanation: Because protective sensation is reduced, injuries can occur unnoticed and progress to severe ulcers without daily visual checks. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h8)

question: Which nursing intervention is most appropriate for a patient experiencing bilateral foot numbness and loss of position sense?

options.A: Encouraging barefoot walking indoors to stimulate proprioceptive feedback
options.B: Applying tight elastic bandages around the toes to improve circulation
options.C: Applying heating pads to the feet for thirty minutes every evening
options.D: Instructing the patient to look at the floor while walking to maintain balance

explanation: Visual cues compensate for lost proprioception and help prevent falls when walking with impaired position sense. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h8)

question: What severe complication can arise from repetitive, unnoticed trauma to an insensate foot?

options.A: Rapid healing of superficial skin abrasions

explanation: Lack of protective sensation allows minor injuries to worsen into deep ulcers and bone infections without the patient noticing. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h9)

question: What factor most heavily influences the long-term prognosis of a patient with peripheral neuropathy?

options.A: Early identification and control of the underlying cause
options.B: Complete bed rest to prevent any further movement
options.C: Complete surgical removal of affected nerve trunks
options.D: High-dose vitamin therapy administered only once a year

explanation: Controlling the primary driver, such as blood sugar in diabetes, halts further nerve destruction and improves long-term outcomes. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h9)
